abstract: We study the support complexity of approximate correlated equilibria (CE) in two-player games, that is, the minimum number of pure action profiles that must be assigned positive probability to approximate a correlated equilibrium of a two-player matrix game. For $\varepsilon$-approximate coarse correlated equilibria, constant approximation is possible with support $O(\log N/\varepsilon^2)$ in $N\times N$ games. For correlated equilibria, the best known upper bound was $O(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ [Babichenko et al., 2014, 2017], but whether this bound was tight remained open. We establish a matching lower bound, resolving the open question of Ko and Schvartzman [2017]. Specifically, we show that, already for two-player zero-sum games, for every $1\leq k\leq N^{1/2}$ the worst-case correlated-equilibrium gap achievable by a distribution supported on at most $k$ pure profiles is $$ Θ\left( \min\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{k^{1/4}}\right\} \right), $$ which implies a $Θ(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ worst-case support bound. The proof builds on a probabilistic-method construction based on random sign matrices.
